interactive.title: The frequency sweep
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in twelve small screens on one picture, the frequency sweep. At the top, a 2 Ω resistor, lesson 4's coil of about 31.8 mH and lesson 5's capacitor of about 318.3 µF sit in series on a 10 V test supply whose frequency can be turned. They are example values, picked so the coil and the capacitor are each exactly 10 Ω at 50 Hz. An ammeter reads the current, and meters read the voltage across each part; like any AC meter, they read rms. In the middle, as in lesson 6, one current flows through every part, so its arrow is the reference and lies flat, and the resistor's arrow lies flat with it. The coil's reactance arrow, X_L, points straight up, because its voltage peaks a quarter cycle before the current (lesson 4). The capacitor's, X_C, points straight down, because its voltage peaks a quarter cycle after the current (lesson 5). The two lie on one line, so tip to tail they leave only their difference, the net reactance X = X_L − X_C, drawn as a third arrow: up when the coil's is longer, down when the capacitor's is. The net arrow and R close lesson 6's triangle, whose long side is the impedance, Z = √(R² + X²), and the current is 10 V ÷ Z. Below, a plot of current against frequency, from 10 to 100 Hz, has a dot at the present frequency that leaves a trace as it moves. Readouts give the current and the voltages across the coil and the capacitor, each the current times that part's reactance. Screen 1 opens at 25 Hz, with X_L and X_C drawn faintly until they grow, and the 2 Ω resistor's arrow short beside them, true to scale. X_L is 5 Ω, half its 50 Hz value, because X_L = 2πfL grows in step with the frequency. X_C is 20 Ω, double its 50 Hz value, because X_C = 1/(2πfC) shrinks as the frequency rises. The two arrows point opposite ways along one line. Screen 2 asks for the net reactance at 25 Hz: 15 Ω, pointing down; 25 Ω (the two added as plain numbers); or 20.6 Ω (the two added at right angles by Pythagoras, as lesson 6 added R and X). A right Check lays the arrows tip to tail, leaving 15 Ω pointing down, then closes the triangle: Z = √(2² + 15²) = 15.1 Ω, and the current is 0.66 A. Screen 3 frees a frequency slider, 10 to 100 Hz in steps of 5, opening at 25. As the frequency rises the X_L arrow grows and the X_C arrow shrinks, so the net arrow shortens, vanishes at 50 Hz and then grows upwards. Z swings down to the 2 Ω of R alone and up again, and the dot traces a peak: 0.21 A at 10 Hz, 2.03 A at 40 Hz, 5 A at 50 Hz, 2.39 A at 60 Hz and 0.66 A at 100 Hz. A small label by the current says it leads the supply's voltage below 50 Hz, is in step at 50 Hz and lags above. Screen 4 sets 75 Hz, where X_L is 15 Ω and X_C is 6.67 Ω, and asks how the current sits against the supply's voltage: it lags, because the net 8.33 Ω points up and the circuit acts like a resistor and a coil; it leads (the capacitor's way round); or it is in step. A right Check shows the net arrow up and φ = 76.5°. Screen 5 finds the peak's frequency without the slider. The current is greatest where X_L = X_C, so set 2πfL = 1/(2πfC). Multiply both sides by f, divide both by 2πL and take the square root: f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)). With this coil and capacitor it gives 50 Hz, where the dot's peak sits. Screen 6: a 100 mH coil and a 10 µF capacitor in series; where do they resonate? Near 159 Hz; near 0.159 Hz (10 µF put in as 10 F); or near 159,000 Hz (the square root left out). A right Check works the line: L × C = 0.1 × 0.00001 = 0.000001, its square root is 0.001, so f₀ = 1/(2π × 0.001) = 159.15 Hz. Screen 7 stops at 50 Hz and multiplies every arrow by the 5 A current, turning ohms into volts, the reverse of lesson 6's step. Below the plot, four bars stand side by side: the supply's 10 V, the resistor's 10 V, the coil's 50 V and the capacitor's 50 V. The coil's and the capacitor's bars pass the supply's and turn red as a warning, because the 5 A peak current flows through each part's 10 Ω. Their arrows, 50 V up and 50 V down, cancel, leaving the resistor's 10 V to match the supply. A line names the ratio, 50 ÷ 10 = 5, as the Q factor; the supply's voltage is then I × R and the coil's I × X_L, so the current cancels and Q = X_L ÷ R. The words add that on the job each part in such a circuit must be rated for Q times the supply, not the supply alone. Moving the slider shows the bars fall back either side of 50 Hz. With 2 Ω, though, the capacitor's stays above the supply's at every setting below 70 Hz, only just at 10 Hz, and the coil's at every setting above 35 Hz: the warning is greatest at resonance but not only there. Screen 8, at 50 Hz: the coil reads 50 V and the capacitor 50 V on a 10 V supply; how? Their voltages are half a cycle apart, so at every instant one cancels the other and the loop still adds up to the supply's; one meter must be faulty, since in series no part can read more than the supply; or the coil and the capacitor make voltage of their own, like a second supply. A right Check plays the coil's and the capacitor's voltage waves on one time axis: each peaks at 70.7 V, which is 50 V × √2, at opposite instants, and their sum stays at zero. Screen 9 frees an R slider, 1 to 10 Ω in steps of 1, opening at 2, beside the frequency slider, and the trace redraws for each R. The peak stays at 50 Hz, because R appears nowhere in f₀; R sets the peak's height, 10 V ÷ R, and its sharpness. At 1 Ω the peak is 10 A, the coil and the capacitor read 100 V each and Q is 10, while at 40 Hz the current is only 2.17 A. At 10 Ω the peak is 1 A, each part reads 10 V and Q is 1, while at 40 Hz the current is still 0.91 A: a low, broad hump. Screen 10 asks what doubling R from 2 Ω to 4 Ω does to the peak: it stays at 50 Hz, and the current there falls to 2.5 A and the coil's reading to 25 V; it moves to a lower frequency; or it moves to a higher frequency and stays at 5 A. A right Check draws both traces. Screens 11 and 12 are mixed. Screen 11: a 6 Ω resistor, a coil of 20 Ω reactance and a capacitor of 12 Ω reactance in series on 230 V, 50 Hz mains; what current flows? 23 A, through X = 8 Ω and Z = 10 Ω; 11.0 A (lesson 6's formula with the coil alone, Z = 20.9 Ω); or 7.06 A (the reactances added, Z = 32.6 Ω). A right Check adds that the coil then carries 23 × 20 = 460 V and the capacitor 23 × 12 = 276 V, both above the 230 V supply. Screen 12 takes a City & Guilds 2366 sample question's circuit: a 40 Ω resistor, a 50 mH coil and a 60 µF capacitor in series on 230 V, 50 Hz; what current flows? 4.20 A, from X_L = 15.71 Ω, X_C = 53.05 Ω, X = 15.71 − 53.05 = −37.34 Ω and Z = √(40² + 37.34²) = 54.72 Ω, so I = 230 ÷ 54.72 = 4.20 A; 3.46 A (the coil left out, lesson 6's formula with the capacitor alone, Z = 66.44 Ω); or 3.85 A (60 µF put in as 60 Ω, Z = 59.68 Ω). A right Check adds that the current leads by 43.0° and that this circuit resonates near 91.9 Hz, so at 50 Hz it is below resonance, the capacitor's reactance is the larger and the current leads. The closing line says the coil and the capacitor cancel each other's voltage in the loop, but each part still carries its own, and that lesson 8 turns to power.
interactive.ignores: The resistor is pure and the coil and the capacitor are ideal, so the arrows sit exactly up and down; a real coil's own wire resistance belongs in R, where it lowers and widens the peak. The supply is a pure sine held at 10 V at every frequency, and the meters are ideal and read rms. Nothing physical points up or down: the directions stand for timing. The picture shows the circuit once it has settled; the build-up after switching on is left out. An iron-cored coil's inductance changes with its current, so a real circuit's resonance can shift a little with the load. A coil or capacitor whose insulation cannot take its voltage at resonance can fail, which the red bars only warn of. A coil and a capacitor side by side, in parallel, behave differently and are not shown. The parts, the supplies and the readings are example values.

explain.text:
Put a coil and a capacitor in the same series loop and their reactances do not add: one takes away from the other, because the coil's voltage peaks a quarter cycle before the current and the capacitor's a quarter cycle after it. As the frequency rises the coil's reactance grows and the capacitor's shrinks, so at one frequency they are equal and cancel. There the circuit's only opposition is its resistance, the current peaks, and the coil and the capacitor can each carry several times the supply's voltage.

One current flows through every part of a series loop, so, as in lesson 6, the current is the reference. The coil's voltage leads the current,[^3] by a quarter cycle (lesson 4), and the capacitor's voltage lags it,[^4] by a quarter cycle (lesson 5). So the two are half a cycle apart: whenever the coil's voltage pushes one way round the loop, the capacitor's pushes the other way. Drawn as arrows, the coil's points straight up and the capacitor's straight down, on one line, so tip to tail they leave only their difference. That difference is the net reactance, X = X_L − X_C, and it takes the place of the single reactance in lesson 6's triangle: Z = √(R² + X²).[^5] On the bench at 25 Hz, the coil's 5 Ω up and the capacitor's 20 Ω down leave 15 Ω pointing down, so with 2 Ω of resistance Z = √(2² + 15²) = 15.1 Ω. When the capacitor's reactance is the larger, the net arrow points down and the circuit behaves like lesson 6's resistor and capacitor, with the current leading; when the coil's is larger, it behaves like a resistor and a coil, with the current lagging.

Now turn the frequency up. The coil's reactance, X_L = 2πfL,[^6] grows in step with the frequency, and the capacitor's, X_C = 1/(2πfC), shrinks as it rises,[^7] so the net arrow shortens, vanishes and then grows the other way. Where it vanishes, X_L = X_C, Z has fallen to R alone, its smallest, and the current is at its greatest.[^8] This is [[resonance]], and the frequency where it happens is the [[resonant frequency]], f₀. Setting 2πf₀L = 1/(2πf₀C) and solving for f₀ gives f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)). Lesson 4's coil and lesson 5's capacitor are each 10 Ω at 50 Hz, so in series they resonate at 50 Hz, and with 2 Ω on a 10 V supply the current peaks at 10 ÷ 2 = 5 A, in step with the supply's voltage, as if the coil and the capacitor were not there. R appears nowhere in f₀, so changing it does not move the peak; it sets how tall the peak is, V ÷ R. Well away from f₀ the net reactance, which R does not touch, makes up most of Z, so there the current hardly changes with a small R; a smaller R lifts only the top, making the peak taller and narrower.

That peak current still flows through the coil and the capacitor, each still 10 Ω. So each carries 5 A × 10 Ω = 50 V, five times the supply's 10 V. The two 50 V voltages are half a cycle apart, so they cancel in the loop, leaving the resistor's 10 V to match the supply. At resonance the supply's voltage equals the resistor's, I × R, while the coil's is I × X_L, so the current cancels from their ratio: the ratio of either part's voltage to the supply's is the circuit's [[Q factor]], X_L ÷ R, here 10 ÷ 2 = 5: the voltage across the coil or the capacitor in a series resonant circuit is Q times the supply's,[^9] which can make it dangerously high.[^10] This is a simplified model, with ideal parts on a pure sine; a real coil's wire resistance adds to R, which lowers and widens the peak without moving it. **In series, a coil's and a capacitor's reactances subtract, so at the resonant frequency, where X_L = X_C, the impedance falls to R alone and the current peaks,[^8] and the voltage across each of them is Q times the supply's.[^9]**

analogy.text: Push a child on a swing. Small pushes timed to the swing's own rhythm build a big, fast swing; push faster or slower than that rhythm and some of your pushes land against it, so it stays small. More friction at the pivot keeps the swing slower, but the rhythm that builds the fastest swing is still set by the length of the chains. Your rhythm of pushing is the supply's frequency, the swing's speed is the current, and the friction is the resistance.
analogy.breaks: The swing does have a match for the big part voltages: it climbs far higher than any one push could lift it, as the capacitor's voltage climbs past the supply's, and gravity's pull and the swing's own inertia grow with it and cancel each other, like the coil's and the capacitor's voltages, leaving your pushes to make up only the friction, as the supply makes up only R. Where it breaks: a swing is one object trading height for speed, while the circuit has two separate parts, the coil and the capacitor, handing energy back and forth between them. And the swing takes short shoves, many of them, to build up, where the supply pushes smoothly all the time and the meters here show the circuit once it has settled.

practice.text:
- Safety first: near resonance the coil and the capacitor can each carry far more than the supply's voltage,[^10] so before a coil and a capacitor in series go live, check each one's voltage rating against at least Q times the supply, not the supply alone,[^9] and √2 times that if it is rated in peak volts. A 6 Ω resistor with 20 Ω of coil reactance and 12 Ω of capacitor reactance on 230 V mains[^1] draws 23 A, and puts 23 × 20 = 460 V across the coil. Isolate, prove dead and discharge any capacitor before handling either part.
- Each reactance: X_L = 2πfL[^6] and X_C = 1/(2πfC),[^7] with f in hertz, L in henries and C in farads (10 µF is 0.00001 F).
- The net reactance: X = X_L − X_C. If it comes out positive the circuit is inductive and the current lags; negative, capacitive, and the current leads.
- The impedance: Z = √(R² + X²).[^5]
- The current: I = V ÷ Z. Each part's voltage is then I times its own R, X_L or X_C.
- The resonant frequency: f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)). There Z = R, the current is V ÷ R[^8] and Q = X_L ÷ R.
- A City & Guilds 2366 sample question puts a 40 Ω resistor, a 50 mH coil and a 60 µF capacitor in series on 230 V, 50 Hz.[^11] X_L = 15.71 Ω and X_C = 53.05 Ω, so X = −37.34 Ω, Z = √(40² + 37.34²) = 54.72 Ω and I = 230 ÷ 54.72 = 4.20 A, leading by 43.0°. It resonates at 91.9 Hz.

**Rule of thumb:** With a coil and a capacitor in series, take the smaller reactance from the larger first, then use Pythagoras with R. Near resonance, when X_L is more than R, expect the coil's and the capacitor's meters to read more than the supply's.

**Worked example:** Lesson 4's coil and lesson 5's capacitor in series with 2 Ω, on a 10 V test supply at 50 Hz: X_L = X_C = 10 Ω, so X = 0, Z = 2 Ω and I = 5 A, in step with the supply. Each part reads 5 × 10 = 50 V, and Q = 10 ÷ 2 = 5. Move the same circuit to 60 Hz, the frequency most common on board ship:[^2] X_L rises to 12 Ω and X_C falls to 8.33 Ω, so X = 3.67 Ω, inductive. Z = √(2² + 3.67²) = 4.18 Ω, I = 10 ÷ 4.18 = 2.39 A, lagging, and the coil reads 2.39 × 12 = 28.7 V, still nearly three times the supply.

Lesson 8 turns to power, where the angle between the current and the voltage decides how much is really used.

**Common mistakes**
- Using lesson 6's formula with one reactance, leaving the coil or the capacitor out.
- Adding X_L and X_C, or putting both under Pythagoras with R. They point opposite ways, so take one from the other first.
- Putting C in as ohms or in microfarads. 100 µF is not 100 Ω; convert it to farads and work out X_C.
- Thinking no part in series can read more than the supply. True of resistors, or of R with just a coil or just a capacitor, but not of a coil and a capacitor together, above all near resonance.
- Thinking R moves the resonant frequency. It changes the peak's height and sharpness, not where it sits.

checks.label: Inductive reactance can be calculated using this formula: X_L = 2πfL. The bench coil is 10 Ω at 50 Hz, and the drawn X_L arrow follows the formula at every setting of the sweep

Capacitive reactance can be calculated using this formula: X_C = 1/(2πfC), and it decreases with increasing frequency: the bench capacitor is 10 Ω at 50 Hz, and the drawn X_C arrow follows the formula and shrinks at every step up the sweep

Because the phasors for reactances are 90° out of phase with the current, the series impedance of a resistor R and a reactance X is given by Pythagoras' law: with X = X_L − X_C, the drawn Z is √(R² + X²) on every screen, at every frequency and at every resistance

Resonance occurs at the frequency where the current has its maximum value, where the impedance is at its minimum, which occurs when X_L = X_C: for every resistance from 1 to 10 Ω the greatest current of the sweep is at 50 Hz, where the drawn X_L and X_C arrows are equal, Z = R and the trace peaks

A practical application of Q is that voltage across L or C in a series resonant circuit is Q times total applied voltage: at 50 Hz with 1, 2, 4 and 10 Ω, Q = X_L ÷ R is 10, 5, 2.5 and 1, and the coil's and the capacitor's meters read Q × 10 V

Because of the high currents which may be present in a series LC circuit at resonance, it is possible to produce dangerously high voltage drops: at 50 Hz the coil and the capacitor read 50 V each on the 10 V supply, and their bars turn red exactly when they pass the supply's, the capacitor's at every setting below 70 Hz and the coil's at every setting above 35 Hz
UK mains electricity operates at a nominal voltage of 230V: on 230 V, 6 Ω with 20 Ω and 12 Ω of reactance draws 23 A and puts 460 V across the coil and 276 V across the capacitor

A 230 V, 50 Hz, AC circuit contains a 40 Ω resistor in series with a 50 mH inductor and a 60 µF capacitor: X_L = 15.71 Ω, X_C = 53.05 Ω, X = −37.34 Ω, Z = 54.72 Ω and 4.20 A flows, leading by 43.0°; it resonates at 91.9 Hz

Known answers: 0.21 A at 10 Hz, 2.03 A at 40 Hz, 5 A at 50 Hz, 2.39 A at 60 Hz and 0.66 A at 25 and 100 Hz; at 25 Hz X = −15 Ω and Z = 15.1 Ω; at 75 Hz X = 8.33 Ω and φ = 76.5°; at 60 Hz the coil reads 28.7 V; with 1 Ω and 10 Ω, 2.17 A and 0.91 A at 40 Hz; 100 mH and 10 µF resonate at 159.15 Hz; 50 mH and 60 µF at 91.9 Hz
The note by the ammeter says the current leads the supply below 50 Hz, is in step with it at 50 Hz and lags above, at every setting of the sweep
Screen 8's waves: the coil's and the capacitor's voltages each peak at 70.7 V, which is 50 V × √2, at opposite instants (0 and 10 ms), and their sum is zero at every drawn instant

On the volts screen every arrow is its ohms times the current: at 50 Hz, 5 A turns 10 Ω into 50 V up and 50 V down, which cancel, and 2 Ω into the resistor's 10 V, equal to the supply's, at every setting

applied.problem: Three overreaches: Q times the supply is not the worst case (at Q 1 the coil reaches 11.5 V on 10 V off resonance; a peak rating needs √2 more); with Q 1 or less nothing reads above the supply at resonance; and series parts on DC never exceed the supply.
